node.label: Lynn Abrams
node.date_label: The Orphan Country (1998) · Myth and Materiality (2005) · Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) · Feminist Lives (2023)
node.description: Lynn Abrams argues in Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) that oral testimony must be interpreted as a communicative encounter: historians need to ask how and why a story is told as well as what it reports. The work connects interviewing with the analysis of memory, narrative and relations between interviewer and narrator. Ronald J. Grele’s 2011 review praised its broad synthesis while noting its limited engagement with folklore. Abrams’s Feminist Lives (2023) asks how a postwar generation of British women made autonomous selves before and alongside organised women’s liberation, including through the expression of feelings. In her 2025 interview, she qualifies the reach of her own interviews: the women were white and mostly middle class by the time she spoke with them. Her work connects women’s and gender history with child welfare, Shetland society and everyday life in Scotland.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Orphan Country (1998); The Making of Modern Woman: Europe 1789–1918 (2002); Myth and Materiality in a Woman’s World: Shetland 1800–2000 (2005); Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016); A History of Everyday Life in Twentieth-Century Scotland (2010), co-edited with Callum G. Brown; Feminist Lives (2023).
node.scope_note: Complete 2025 interview, public publisher chapter summaries, book and chapter abstracts, university bibliography and selected endorsements read. Grele is read only through the publisher-indexed opening extract. Monographs, full book chapters, Grele’s full review and Portelli’s 2011 review are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková, Abrams identifies Summerfield’s theoretically informed feminist oral history as an influence on her own approach.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 153, first answer to “Who influenced”: “I was influenced” and “I read all her work.” This is Abrams’s own attribution; no individual Summerfield title is specified there. Summerfield’s separate publisher endorsement of the first edition is also read, but does not date the original influence. Her works were not independently read for this packet.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková, Abrams names reading Portelli among the influences on her understanding of oral history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 153, answer to “Who influenced”, names Portelli alongside Summerfield, Frisch and Daniel James. The retrospective answer supports a limited reading debt; no particular Portelli work or sole theoretical derivation is specified. Portelli’s own texts and his 2011 review of Abrams remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Abrams and Callum G. Brown co-edited A History of Everyday Life in Twentieth-Century Scotland (2010) and jointly wrote its introduction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: EUP publisher record, editor byline, Contents chapter 1, and February 2010 publication dates; Glasgow publication list, 2010 entries, identifies “Introduction: conceiving the everyday in the twentieth century”, pp. 1–19. Verified collaboration only; neither equal division of intellectual labour nor an argument from the unread introduction is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016) links interview practice to analysis of how, why and with what meaning testimony is produced.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher companion Chapter 1, Chapter summary, paragraphs 1–3: interviews are a “communicative event”. The 2016 summary directly supplies this interpretation; the interview p. 151 and note 7 establish the original 2010 and second-edition 2016 dates. Full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Oral History Theory (2010; second edition 2016), Abrams treats remembering as an active process and asks historians to interpret relations between individual and collective memory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2016 publisher companion Chapter 5, Chapter summary, paragraphs 1–3, and Discussion points 4–6. Exact phrase: “Memory is an active process”. This supports the second-edition formulation, not a claim that every passage appeared in 2010. Reliability questions are reweighted, not declared irrelevant to establishing events. Full chapter unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Feminist Lives (2023) uses women’s testimony to explain how a postwar transition generation fashioned autonomous selves before and alongside the Women’s Liberation Movement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: OUP book Abstract, both paragraphs, describes the transition generation and challenges its neglect as insufficiently feminist. Interview pp. 155 and 162–163 supplies authorial explanation and sample limits: her own interviewees were white and mostly middle class by interview time. The full book is unread; this is a scoped contribution, not a representative account of every British woman.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Introduction: Gendering the Agenda” (2006), Abrams proposes using women’s history and the analysis of gender relations to reinterpret Scottish history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Public chapter Abstract, entire paragraph: “shift the agenda”. Original chapter dated 25 January 2006; book abstract lists politics, identity, work and religion as gendered subjects. Claim stays within the abstract; chapter body and named theoretical debts within it are unread. Four-editor collection credited separately.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Feminist Lives (2023), Abrams argues that expressing and acting on feelings helped postwar British women construct new selves.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview p. 155, answer on the connection between feelings and self, and p. 161, answer on archival research. Abrams links emotion to feminist self formation and says organisational correspondence made that dimension visible. The OUP abstract confirms the work and date. Distinct from the women’s-history link: this claim concerns feelings as historical action and evidence. Full book unread; no derivation from Reddy or Rosenwein inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2025 interview with Marie Jiřičková discussing Feminist Lives (2023), Abrams reverses Sara Ahmed’s formulation of feminism as an emotional response to the world, describing emotion as a feminist response to the world.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 155, answer to the question about feelings and the self in Feminist Lives. Abrams explicitly attributes the first formulation to Ahmed, reverses its terms, and then explains how postwar British women’s expression of feelings helped constitute a new self. This is named engagement with an argument in a published interview. The interview prints Ahmed’s first name as Sarah; the feminist theorist of emotion is identified here with the supplied run member Sara Ahmed. The supporting phrase preserves the printed spelling. The relationship is a comparison because the passage reformulates the proposition without asserting a broader disagreement. No specific Ahmed book is named in this passage, and neither Ahmed’s underlying text nor Feminist Lives was read for this backfill.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reverses the formulation of feminism and emotion

proposed_edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to labour history in Workers' Culture in Imperial Germany: Leisure and Recreation in the Rhineland and Westphalia (1992), interpreting workers' leisure in Bochum and Düsseldorf as an arena of assertiveness under bourgeois pressure to reform popular recreation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete substantive annotation on printed p. 296 in the journal publisher's PDF. It identifies Abrams's book, its original 1992 publication and geographical scope, and describes her interpretation of workers' response to attempts to reform recreation. Labour-history classification is an editorial mapping of this stated argument to the existing field, whose scope includes workers' culture beyond formal labour organisations. The annotation is evidence of the book's argument and reception; the book itself remains unread. No claim of founding the field or subsequent personal influence is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to the history of everyday life through A History of Everyday Life in Twentieth-Century Scotland (2010), co-edited with Callum G. Brown, which examines mundane practices and daily spaces as sites of personal and national politics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's complete description, editor credits, contents and original publication dates. The description explicitly treats apparently mundane activities and daily spaces as historical inquiries into politics. Abrams is both co-editor and a credited coauthor of the introduction and the chapter on the Scottish home. This field edge records her contribution through a substantive edited research collection, with credit retained for Brown and the other contributors. The target is the existing combined 'Microhistory / everyday life' node, specifically its everyday-life component; the evidence does not establish Italian microstoria affiliation or transmission from a particular school. Full chapters remain unread. The existing Abrams–Brown pair is not proposed again.

proposed_edges.relationship: Lynn Abrams contributes to urban history through Glasgow: High-Rise Homes, Estates and Communities in the Post-War Period (2020), coauthored with Ade Kearns, Barry Hazley and Valerie Wright, connecting architectural design and planning with residents' housing experiences through oral histories and archival materials.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete four-paragraph abstract and bibliographic record deposited by Abrams in her own institution's repository. The second paragraph specifies oral histories and archival materials, the third states the analytical connection, and the fourth explicitly names urban historians among the book's audience. This supports a contribution about housing, built environments and residents' experience, rather than mere shared subject matter. The record gives 2020 and first online publication on 7 July 2020. No book text is supplied there and the full book remains unread. The collective argument is attributed to all four authors; the other authors have no matching timeline endpoint in the supplied lists.
